conditions.name: Plague, including pneumonic plague
conditions.overview: Original board-study material on CDC plague treatment and prevention recommendations. Distinguish the clinical form, severity and population before selecting an answer. This is study material, not patient-care guidance, official ABFM content or clinician-approved commercial reference material.

sources.title: Antimicrobial Treatment and Prophylaxis of Plague: Recommendations for Naturally Acquired Infections and Bioterrorism Response
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Introduction: clinical manifestations and transmission; Recommendations: adult/child treatment, pneumonic/septicemic, bubonic/pharyngeal and meningeal plague, prophylaxis, pregnant women; Tables 1–5. Each study section has a specific sourceLocator.
sources.limitations: CDC recommendations, not independent clinical approval. Adult first-line lists must not be extended to pregnancy or neonates. The guideline excludes detailed diagnostic-testing and triage protocols. No dose tables or third-party works are imported.

sections.title: Recognize the form of plague
sections.text: Yersinia pestis causes plague. Infection can follow infected flea bites, contact with infected tissues or fluids, or inhalation of infectious droplets. Bubonic plague produces a tender swollen lymph node, or bubo. Primary pneumonic plague follows inhalation and can present with fever, dyspnea and, later, purulent or bloody sputum. Untreated pneumonic disease can progress rapidly to respiratory failure and sepsis; prompt antimicrobial treatment is essential.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction — Plague Pathogenesis and Clinical Manifestations; paragraphs on transmission, bubonic plague and primary pneumonic plague.

sections.title: First-line antibiotics for adult pneumonic or septicemic plague
sections.text: In CDC Table 1, the first-line agents for adults aged at least 18 years with pneumonic or septicemic plague are ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin and streptomycin. These are multiple recommended options, not a single universally best drug. Route and selection depend on severity, ability to tolerate oral medication and individual factors. Pregnancy and neonatal recommendations require their separate source sections; this adult list does not establish their regimen.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Antimicrobial Treatment of Adults and Children; Table 1, Adults aged ≥18 years, First-line category; separate special-population recommendations.

sections.title: Doxycycline depends on the clinical form
sections.text: CDC classifies doxycycline as an alternative for pneumonic or septicemic plague, but as a first-line option for bubonic or pharyngeal plague. A stable patient with naturally acquired primary bubonic or pharyngeal disease and no secondary pneumonic or septicemic involvement can receive one recommended antimicrobial. Progression to pneumonic or septicemic disease changes which treatment recommendations apply. Do not transfer the bubonic first-line designation to pneumonic plague.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Pneumonic and Septicemic Plague, doxycycline discussion; Bubonic and Pharyngeal Plague, opening and final paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2.

sections.title: Severity changes the treatment strategy
sections.text: When the clinical and exposure history clearly indicates naturally occurring plague, CDC allows consideration of a single recommended agent for mild-to-moderate pneumonic or septicemic disease. Severe pneumonic or septicemic plague calls for two distinct antimicrobial classes initially, with narrowing to one agent after clinical improvement. This differs from treating every plague presentation with monotherapy regardless of severity.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Pneumonic and Septicemic Plague; paragraphs beginning 'If clinical and exposure history clearly indicate naturally occurring plague' and 'For patients with severe septicemic or pneumonic disease'.

sections.title: Preserve community-acquired pneumonia coverage when uncertain
sections.text: If naturally occurring pneumonic plague is being considered but the diagnosis is uncertain, CDC recommends including coverage for community-acquired pneumonia until diagnostic results are available. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin are identified as particularly useful options in this circumstance. This is a diagnostic-uncertainty recommendation, not a claim that every pneumonia is plague or that one drug fits every patient.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Pneumonic and Septicemic Plague; paragraphs on uncertain diagnosis and levofloxacin or moxifloxacin.

sections.title: Duration and route are conditional
sections.text: CDC recommends a total treatment duration of 10–14 days generally across clinical forms, with extension considered for ongoing fever or other concerning findings. Parenteral versus oral treatment depends on severity and whether oral medication is tolerated. An initial intravenous regimen can be changed to oral treatment when clinical improvement is apparent and the treating team considers that appropriate. These general statements do not supply patient-specific doses or remove drug-specific restrictions. Secondary plague meningitis has a separate recommendation to continue the entire regimen for an additional 10 days after the indicated antimicrobial is added.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Antimicrobial Treatment of Adults and Children; final paragraphs on route transition and 10–14-day total treatment.; Meningeal Plague, secondary-meningitis paragraphs; Table 3 footnote.

sections.title: Meningitis requires its own regimen
sections.text: For plague presenting with signs of meningitis, CDC recommends initial dual treatment with chloramphenicol plus moxifloxacin or levofloxacin when possible. If chloramphenicol is unavailable, the guideline permits substitution of a nonfluoroquinolone first-line or alternative agent used for septicemic plague. This meningeal recommendation must not be replaced by the routine single-agent strategy for stable bubonic disease.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Meningeal Plague; Table 3 and its dual-therapy footnote.

sections.title: Pneumonic transmission and droplet precautions
sections.text: Pneumonic plague is the clinical form that can spread person to person through large respiratory droplets. CDC calls for respiratory droplet precautions when caring for patients with pneumonic plague. The guideline reports no evidence of the airborne transmission pattern seen with measles. Keep this distinction tied to plague; it does not redefine precautions for other respiratory infections.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction — Person-to-Person Transmission of Plague; opening paragraph on large droplets, droplet precautions and absence of evidence for airborne transmission.

sections.title: Exposure prophylaxis is separate from treatment
sections.text: CDC says to consider postexposure prophylaxis after close, sustained contact within 6 feet of a person with pneumonic plague without adequate personal protective equipment. Certain accidental laboratory exposures and close or direct contact with infected animals are also considered. The recommended postexposure course is 7 days. Health care personnel who maintained standard and droplet precautions do not routinely need this prophylaxis. An exposure scenario is different from symptomatic infection requiring treatment.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Antimicrobial Pre- and Postexposure Prophylaxis; paragraphs on close sustained contact, 7 days and appropriately protected health care personnel; Table 4.

sections.title: Pregnancy does not justify delaying indicated treatment
sections.text: CDC states that fetal safety concerns should not prevent rapid, effective treatment or prophylaxis for affected pregnant women when indicated. Selection still requires pregnancy-specific safety and effectiveness considerations; the ordinary adult first-line list is not a substitute for those recommendations. The guideline acknowledges limited pregnancy evidence, including case-report limitations. This module does not provide a complete pregnancy or neonatal prescribing protocol.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Antimicrobial Treatment and Prophylaxis of Special Populations, Pregnant Women; opening paragraphs on rapid treatment, effectiveness and evidence limitations; Table 5.

questions.stem: In a fictional board vignette, a 34-year-old nonpregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired pneumonic plague. Relevant medication allergies and contraindications are absent. Which drug is in the CDC adult FIRST-LINE category for pneumonic plague? This question asks for the category, not a complete patient-specific regimen.

choices.text: Doxycycline
Levofloxacin
Azithromycin
Metronidazole
Vancomycin

questions.explanation: CDC Table 1 places levofloxacin among first-line adult agents for pneumonic or septicemic plague. Doxycycline is an alternative for these forms. Severity still determines whether one agent or two distinct classes are appropriate.

distractorExplanations.A: Doxycycline is listed as an alternative for pneumonic or septicemic plague; its first-line designation for bubonic or pharyngeal disease does not answer this question.
distractorExplanations.C: Azithromycin is not in the Table 1 first-line adult list.
distractorExplanations.D: Metronidazole is not in the Table 1 first-line adult list.
distractorExplanations.E: Vancomycin is not in the Table 1 first-line adult list.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish first-line adult pneumonic-plague agents from alternatives without assuming a universal regimen.

questions.stem: A fictional nonpregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired pneumonic plague with severe respiratory illness. There is no meningeal involvement and effective drugs from different classes are available. Which initial antimicrobial STRATEGY follows CDC guidance for severe pneumonic plague?

choices.text: Use no antibiotics until the illness becomes mild
Use a single agent in every case regardless of severity
Use the 7-day exposure-prophylaxis strategy instead of treatment
Start two distinct antimicrobial classes; narrow after clinical improvement
Select a bubonic-only recommendation without considering pulmonary disease

questions.explanation: For severe pneumonic or septicemic plague, CDC recommends initial dual therapy using two distinct antimicrobial classes and narrowing to a single agent after clinical improvement. The mild-to-moderate naturally acquired monotherapy allowance does not fit this severe presentation.

distractorExplanations.A: The source calls for effective treatment of severe disease, not withholding it until severity changes.
distractorExplanations.B: The monotherapy consideration applies to clearly naturally occurring mild-to-moderate disease, not every severity.
distractorExplanations.C: This is symptomatic severe infection, not an exposure-only prophylaxis scenario.
distractorExplanations.E: Pulmonary disease belongs under the pneumonic/septicemic recommendations.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the severe-pneumonic-plague dual-class strategy and its de-escalation condition.

questions.stem: In a fictional exposure vignette, an asymptomatic adult had prolonged close contact within 6 feet of a coughing person with confirmed pneumonic plague and wore no adequate personal protective equipment. Which CDC prevention statement best fits this exposure?

choices.text: Consider postexposure antimicrobial prophylaxis for 7 days
No prophylaxis consideration is needed because the exposed adult has no symptoms
Use a severe-infection dual-class treatment strategy solely because exposure occurred
Treat every protected and unprotected contact identically
Use a single day of prophylaxis

questions.explanation: Close, sustained contact with a pneumonic-plague patient without adequate protection is a CDC postexposure-prophylaxis consideration. CDC recommends 7 days for postexposure prophylaxis. This does not establish a symptomatic-infection treatment regimen.

distractorExplanations.B: Postexposure prevention concerns exposure risk and can apply before symptoms develop.
distractorExplanations.C: The severe-treatment strategy is for severe infection; this vignette describes an asymptomatic exposure.
distractorExplanations.D: CDC distinguishes inadequate protection from health care personnel who maintained standard and droplet precautions.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated CDC postexposure duration is 7 days, not one day.

questions.learningObjective: Separate plague exposure prophylaxis from symptomatic treatment and retain protection criteria.

questions.stem: A fictional adult study case has stable, naturally acquired primary bubonic plague with no secondary pneumonic or septicemic involvement and no relevant drug contraindication. Which statement correctly compares CDC's doxycycline classification across clinical forms?

choices.text: Doxycycline is first-line for every form without qualification
Doxycycline is absent from all CDC plague recommendations
Doxycycline is only an exposure-prophylaxis drug
Doxycycline has the same alternative-only designation for bubonic and pneumonic disease
Doxycycline is first-line for bubonic/pharyngeal disease but alternative for pneumonic/septicemic disease

questions.explanation: The CDC recommendation changes with clinical form: doxycycline is first-line for bubonic or pharyngeal plague and alternative for pneumonic or septicemic plague. Stable naturally acquired bubonic disease without secondary involvement can use a single recommended agent.

distractorExplanations.A: This erases the alternative designation for pneumonic or septicemic disease.
distractorExplanations.B: Doxycycline appears in both treatment tables, with different categories.
distractorExplanations.C: The source includes doxycycline treatment recommendations, not prophylaxis alone.
distractorExplanations.D: Table 2 gives a first-line designation for bubonic or pharyngeal disease.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid transferring a drug's first-line designation between different plague presentations.

conditions.name: Tularemia
conditions.overview: Original board-study material on the CDC 2025 tularemia recommendations. Focus on preferred drugs and how severity, delayed treatment, pregnancy, age and meningitis change the answer. Study use only; no patient-specific prescribing, official ABFM affiliation or clinician-approved commercial reference is asserted.

sources.title: Tularemia Antimicrobial Treatment and Prophylaxis: CDC Recommendations for Naturally Acquired Infections and Bioterrorism Response — United States, 2025
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Introduction; Recommendations: Changes and Updates, Clinical Considerations, Neuroinvasive Tularemia, prophylaxis and Pregnant Women; Box summary; Tables 1–3. Each study section has a specific sourceLocator.
sources.limitations: Treatment selection is conditional, with limited evidence for severe-disease combination benefit. Pregnancy, neonates and neuroinvasive disease have separate recommendations. No drug doses, diagnostic laboratory protocols or unrestricted antibiotic substitutions are supplied.

sections.title: Exposure and clinical pattern
sections.text: Francisella tularensis causes tularemia. Arthropod bites or inoculation through broken skin during contact with infected animal tissues often cause ulceroglandular or glandular disease. Inhalation can cause pneumonic tularemia. Typhoidal disease is systemic and can lack localized findings. The exposure route helps frame a board vignette, but these associations do not themselves confirm a diagnosis or supply a laboratory protocol.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction — opening paragraphs on Francisella tularensis, routes of exposure and route-associated clinical manifestations.

sections.title: First-line treatment and age boundaries
sections.text: CDC's 2025 recommendations list ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and doxycycline as first-line treatment options for adults and children aged at least 1 month. Neonates aged 28 days or younger have a separate first-line list of ciprofloxacin or gentamicin. Selection depends on severity, availability, route and adverse-effect considerations. The adult list is not a blanket pregnancy or neonatal recommendation, and an age between these source-defined groups must not be assigned a regimen by extrapolation.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — Treatment recommendation for adults and children; Table 1 population categories; separate pregnancy and neonatal recommendations.

sections.title: Clinical forms and antibiotics that do not treat tularemia
sections.text: The guideline says ulceroglandular, pneumonic and typhoidal tularemia can be treated with the recommended ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin or doxycycline options; meningitis is a separate exception. Beta-lactams, including penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems, are ineffective for tularemia even when some laboratory susceptibility results appear favorable. Polymyxins, glycopeptides and sulfonamides are also ineffective. Do not substitute a routine beta-lactam regimen for source-supported tularemia treatment.
sections.sourceLocator: Introduction — paragraph listing ineffective antimicrobial classes; Recommendations — Clinical Considerations for Treatment Recommendations, opening paragraph.

sections.title: Severe disease: aminoglycoside consideration, not invented certainty
sections.text: For severe tularemia, indicated by hemodynamic instability, end-organ dysfunction, respiratory-support needs or other sepsis/severe-illness findings, CDC says to consider initial aminoglycoside treatment when possible. Two effective classes, such as gentamicin plus ciprofloxacin, may be considered in selected circumstances. The guideline explicitly states that evidence that initial combination therapy improves severe-tularemia outcomes is minimal. Do not represent optional dual treatment as proven superior for every severe case.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Clinical Considerations for Treatment Recommendations; paragraphs on severe infection, initial aminoglycosides and limited combination-treatment evidence.

sections.title: Delayed treatment changes preference
sections.text: When treatment is delayed, CDC prefers ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin over doxycycline. The clinical-considerations discussion specifically says that a delay greater than 2 weeks supports considering a bactericidal agent, such as ciprofloxacin or gentamicin, over bacteriostatic doxycycline, or considering two-drug combination therapy. This is not a claim that doxycycline is never first-line; it is a preference modified by delay and the clinical situation.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — delayed-treatment bullet; Recommendations — Clinical Considerations for Treatment Recommendations, treatment-delay discussion and paragraph beginning 'During an outbreak of ulceroglandular and typhoidal tularemia in Spain'.

sections.title: General duration and oral transition
sections.text: The general CDC treatment durations are 10 days for ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin and 14–21 days for doxycycline. Persistent fever, abscesses or other concerning findings can justify considering longer treatment. Table 1 permits transition from initial intravenous or intramuscular therapy to an oral regimen after defervescence and clinical improvement, including a change of antimicrobial class if needed. Neuroinvasive disease has separate combination and total-duration recommendations.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — treatment-duration bullet; Table 1 transition-to-oral footnotes; Recommendations — Clinical Considerations, persistent-fever paragraph and Neuroinvasive Tularemia.

sections.title: Pregnancy-specific first-line options
sections.text: For pregnant women with tularemia, CDC recommends ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin as first-line treatment. The choice depends on severity, availability, route and side-effect considerations. Doxycycline's inclusion in the ordinary adult first-line list does not make it first-line in this pregnancy-specific list. Pregnancy postexposure prophylaxis is a different category and uses ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin as the preferred options.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — Treatment recommendation for pregnant women and Postexposure prophylaxis recommendation; Tables 2 and 3.

sections.title: Neuroinvasive disease requires separate combination treatment
sections.text: CDC recommends gentamicin plus ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin for neuroinvasive tularemia. Gentamicin plus doxycycline may be an acceptable alternative when fluoroquinolones are unavailable or contraindicated. The source describes aminoglycoside treatment for at least 10 days in successfully treated cases and continuing treatment to a total of 21 days after transition to oral therapy. Do not replace this recommendation with routine uncomplicated-disease monotherapy or its shorter general duration.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Neuroinvasive Tularemia; final paragraphs on gentamicin combinations, at least 10 days of aminoglycoside treatment and 21-day total treatment.

sections.title: Do not repeat the older streptomycin-first framing
sections.text: The 2025 update moved ciprofloxacin and doxycycline into first-line treatment options and added levofloxacin as first-line. Streptomycin is now a third-tier treatment option because of adverse-event concerns, limited US availability and potential administration errors associated with infrequent use. Third-tier does not mean ineffective: the source acknowledges streptomycin's efficacy. These current recommendation ranks matter more than an unqualified historical drug-of-choice mnemonic.
sections.sourceLocator: Recommendations — Changes and Updates to Previous Recommendations, numbered items 3–5.

sections.title: Keep prophylaxis distinct from treatment
sections.text: For persons whose exposure warrants tularemia postexposure prophylaxis, the Box lists ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or doxycycline for nonpregnant adults, children and neonates, and ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin for pregnant women. Prophylaxis duration is 7 days for ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin and 10–14 days for doxycycline. These exposure-prevention recommendations are not symptomatic-infection treatment durations, and this summary does not establish that every arthropod bite warrants prophylaxis.
sections.sourceLocator: Box — Postexposure prophylaxis recommendation for adults (including pregnant women) and children; Tables 2 and 3.

questions.stem: A fictional nonpregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired tularemia without meningitis. Four first-line options are being reviewed under the CDC 2025 guideline. Which statement accurately describes the CURRENT recommendation categories?

choices.text: Streptomycin is the sole first-line treatment and every other drug is third-tier
Amoxicillin is first-line because all beta-lactams are effective against tularemia
Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and doxycycline are first-line options; streptomycin is third-tier
Doxycycline is never a treatment option in adults
All agents share one recommendation category with no patient-specific modifiers

questions.explanation: The 2025 CDC recommendations list ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin and doxycycline as first-line options for adults and children aged at least 1 month. Streptomycin is third-tier. Severity, delay, pregnancy and neuroinvasive involvement can change selection; first-line status is not a universal patient-specific prescription.

distractorExplanations.A: This repeats an older unqualified framing; streptomycin is third-tier in the 2025 update.
distractorExplanations.B: The guideline states that beta-lactams are ineffective for tularemia.
distractorExplanations.D: Doxycycline is included in the adult first-line list, although some scenarios favor other drugs.
distractorExplanations.E: The source separates first-line, alternative and third-tier categories and includes clinical modifiers.

questions.learningObjective: Use the current CDC tularemia treatment ranking instead of an unsupported historical mnemonic.

questions.stem: In a fictional board case, a nonpregnant adult with confirmed tularemia has had symptoms for 3 weeks without effective antimicrobial treatment. There is no meningitis. When comparing ciprofloxacin with doxycycline and assuming neither is contraindicated, which CDC preference is most relevant?

choices.text: Delay has no role in antimicrobial selection
A bactericidal agent such as ciprofloxacin is favored over doxycycline when treatment has been delayed more than 2 weeks
Ciprofloxacin is never recommended for tularemia
Any beta-lactam automatically replaces the tularemia regimen after 2 weeks
Doxycycline must be selected solely because it appears in the first-line list

questions.explanation: The source's treatment-delay discussion favors considering a bactericidal agent, such as ciprofloxacin or gentamicin, over doxycycline after a delay greater than 2 weeks. The Box also lists ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin as preferred over doxycycline when treatment initiation is delayed.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC explicitly treats delayed effective therapy as a selection modifier.
distractorExplanations.C: Ciprofloxacin is a recommended first-line option.
distractorExplanations.D: Beta-lactams are ineffective for tularemia; delay does not make them a substitute.
distractorExplanations.E: General first-line status does not erase the specific delayed-treatment preference.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the source's delayed-treatment modifier without claiming doxycycline is universally ineffective.

questions.stem: A fictional adult has confirmed severe tularemia with hemodynamic instability. Effective drug options are available and no meningeal involvement is identified. Which statement best preserves both the CDC recommendation and its evidence limitation?

choices.text: Two-drug therapy is proven superior for every severe case
Severe illness never changes the initial antimicrobial approach
Only an oral beta-lactam should be considered
Consider initial aminoglycoside treatment; combination therapy may be considered, but evidence of improved severe-case outcomes is minimal
Apply an asymptomatic exposure-prophylaxis duration as the treatment plan

questions.explanation: CDC says to consider initial aminoglycoside treatment for severe infection when possible. Combination therapy with two effective classes may be considered in selected circumstances, while the source explicitly notes minimal evidence that it improves severe-tularemia outcomes.

distractorExplanations.A: This overstates the limited evidence described by CDC.
distractorExplanations.B: The source specifically discusses an initial aminoglycoside approach for severe disease.
distractorExplanations.C: Beta-lactams are ineffective for tularemia and do not match the severe-disease recommendation.
distractorExplanations.E: Severe symptomatic infection belongs to treatment recommendations, not exposure-only prevention.

questions.learningObjective: Retain the difference between a severe-disease treatment consideration and proven comparative benefit.

questions.stem: In a fictional board question, a pregnant adult has confirmed naturally acquired tularemia without neuroinvasive disease. The question asks for the CDC pregnancy-specific FIRST-LINE treatment set, assuming no relevant contraindications. Which set matches the 2025 recommendations?

choices.text: Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin
Doxycycline alone as the only first-line pregnancy option
Amoxicillin, ceftriaxone or meropenem
Streptomycin alone as the sole first-line option
No antimicrobials for any pregnant patient with tularemia

questions.explanation: The pregnancy-specific Box lists ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or gentamicin as first-line treatment options. Selection still depends on severity and individual considerations. The general nonpregnant adult list must not replace this pregnancy-specific recommendation.

distractorExplanations.B: Doxycycline is not in the pregnancy-specific first-line list.
distractorExplanations.C: These are beta-lactams, which the guideline states are ineffective for tularemia.
distractorExplanations.D: The source's pregnancy-specific first-line list is not streptomycin alone.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC provides antimicrobial treatment recommendations for pregnant women with tularemia.

questions.learningObjective: Keep tularemia's pregnancy-specific first-line treatment set separate from ordinary adult recommendations.
